# Course content:<br> goals and background {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## The core goals of this course

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

This course tries to enable you to...

1. do your research more **reproducibly** and **efficiently**

2. work with large-scale "**omics**" datasets

:::
::: {.column}

. . .

It will focus on general, foundational "**computing skills**".
For example, you will learn to...

- code in the Unix shell and in R
- organize, document, manage, and share your research data, code, and results
- work with a remote supercomputer

:::
:::

## Course background I: Reproducibility

. . .

**Reproducibility and replicability are two related but distinct ideas:**

1. Research is [**replicable**]{.teal} when independent experiments produce the same results
2. Research is [**reproducible**]{.blue} when the same data produce the same results (_a lower bar!_)

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Our focus is on #2.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Course background I: Reproducibility

**In general terms, your research is reproducible when you:**

- Share your data
- Share your methods --- in sufficient detail for anyone to redo what you did
- All reported data, methods and results are congruent

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

> *"The most basic principle for reproducible research is: Do everything via code."*\
> —Karl Broman, University of Madison

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-quiz appearance="simple"}
::: {.callout-note}
#### Can you think of any reasons why this might be true?
{{< fa user-edit >}} *Let's do a Zoom poll*
:::
:::

## Course background I: Reproducibility

**We will cover the following practices that benefit reproducibility:**

- Using code, and following best practices doing so (*throughout*)

. . .

- Detailed project and workflow documentation (*week 2 & week 10*)
- Appropriate and systematic project file organization  (*week 2*)

. . .

- Data and code management & sharing (*weeks 5 & 10*)
- Using open-source software with "containers" (*week 6*)

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . . 

::: callout-tip
##### Another motivator: working reproducibly will benefit future you!

See @markowetz2015's "_Five selfish reasons to work reproducibly_"
in this week's readings.
:::

## Course background II: Efficiency & automation

**Using code also means that you can work more efficiently and improve automation** —\
this can be particularly useful when you have to, for example:

- Do repetitive tasks
- Recreate a figure or redo an analysis after adding a sample

. . .

- Redo all analyses after ... finding a mistake in the first data processing step 😳

## Course background III: Omics data

- The next lecture will give an introduction to omics data.

. . . 

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

- The course will use some example omics datasets,
  but will *not* comprehensively cover how to perform specific omics analyses,
  or its underlying methods ---
  the focus is on foundational computing skills.

. . . 

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

- To learn more about specific omics analyses,
  the following two courses are highly recommended:

  - **Genome Analytics** by Dr. Jonathan Fresnedo-Ramirez (HCS 7004, Spring) 
  - **Microbiome Informatics** by Dr. Matthew Sullivan (MICRO 8161, Fall)

## Recap: course goals and background

This core will focus on teaching you foundational computing skills that enable you to...

- do your research more **reproducibly** and **efficiently**

- work with large-scale "**omics**" datasets

# Course practicalities: <br> homework and grading {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## What your grade is made up of

You can earn a total of 100 points across 5 graded assignments and 4
checkpoints for your final project.

## Graded assignments (50 pts)

A total of 5 graded assignments, worth 10 points each,
are due on Sundays at the end of the following weeks:

<br>

| Nr. | Topic                          |   Due    |
| --- | ------------------------------ | :------: |
| GA1 | Markdown and Unix shell basics |  week 3  |
| GA2 | Unix shell and version control |  week 5  |
| GA3 | Software and shell scripts     |  week 7  |
| GA4 | Slurm batch jobs               | week  9  |
| GA5 | Running Nextflow pipelines     | week  11 |

: {.striped}

## Final project (50 pts)

Plan and implement a small data analysis project --- with checkpoints:

<br>

| Nr. | What              | Due     | Points |
| --- | ----------------- | ------- | :----: |
| FP1 | Proposal          | week 12 |   10   |
| FP2 | Progress report   | week 14 |   10   |
| FP3 | Oral presentation | week 16 |   10   |
| FP4 | Final submission  | week 16 |   20   |

: {.striped}

<br>

. . .

::: callout-tip
#### Datasets for the final project

Ideally, you have or develop your own idea for a dataset and analysis.
That way, you can work on something that's directly useful for your own research.
If not, we can provide you with a dataset.
:::

## Using generative AI for graded assignments

- In week 8, we will cover the use of generative and agentic AI for coding and documentation.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

- **After that**, for some assignments and exercises,
  you are allowed or even encouraged to use AI for these purposes.
  This will be clearly stated on a case-by-case basis.

## Ungraded homework

- **Readings**

- **Exercises** (in weeks with no graded assignment)

- **Ungraded assignments** (occasionally, such as surveys, account setup, etc.)

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

:::callout-warning
#### Always start the week by reading the **week overview** page!  

**Week overviews** will provide a summary of the topics covered in each week,
including any readings, exercises, and assignments.

They will be available by the preceding Friday,
and you are expected to read them before the Monday lecture.
:::

## Readings

In some weeks, specific required readings, such as a paper, will be assigned.
Additionally:

- You are always expected to reread, and practice with, the lecture material

- Some slide decks are accompanied by lecture notes pages,
  which are also required reading

. . .

<br>

::: callout-note
#### Further resources / optional readings

Week overviews list "further resources" (optional readings) for each week.

This often includes chapters from the following two books
(available online through the OSU library):

- @allesina2019: Computing Skills for Biologists
  ([library link {{< fa external-link >}}](https://search.library.osu.edu/permalink/01OHIOLINK_OSU/1oqfg3i/alma991085518416808507){target="_blank"})
- @buffalo2015: Bioinformatics Data Skills
  ([library link {{< fa external-link >}}](https://search.library.osu.edu/permalink/01OHIOLINK_OSU/1oqfg3i/alma991085456156508507){target="_blank"})
:::

## Weekly recitation on Monday

An optional but highly recommended weekly recitation meeting will go over the
exercises or graded assignment for the preceding week.

If you are interested in joining these sessions,
[**please indicate your availability using this poll**](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/r/wqriyRJSmd).

<br>

::: callout-caution
## Practice is key to learn these skills!

This course is intended to be highly practical.
If you don't spend time practicing by yourself,
you may not get much out of it.
:::
